editorial: The opening promises more than the evidence shows. It says Splunk's Kubernetes metrics stayed at available 1 after every one of the five deletions. The body says the chart caught one dip in phase 2, and splunk_k8s_view only measured the two phase-1 deletions. Fix: Limit the opening to what was measured: in the two phase-1 deletions, the 10 s k8s.deployment.available points stayed at 1 while kubectl showed 0 for about 2 s. Mention the one phase-2 dip. Otherwise, add per-deletion Kubernetes measurements for receiver-1..3.

technical: Time not RUNNING is understated when one deletion causes several restarts. analyze.sh takes only the first RESTARTING and the next RUNNING after each deletion, so a deletion that caused 3 restarts is reported as 5.0 s. Fix: Add up every RESTARTING-to-RUNNING interval between one deletion and the next, and publish a phase-2 table with restarts per deletion and total seconds not RUNNING. Rewrite the TL;DR line to match.

technical: Phase 2 changed more than the receiver, and the headline's 7 restarts come from extra restarts per deletion that the post doesn't explain. Phase 1 deletions were 45 s apart and phase 2 deletions 30 s apart. Restarts per deletion went from 1 to 2 or 3 with no cause recorded. Fix: Remove 'the only change' and state the different spacing. Record Flink's /jobs/<jid>/exceptions root cause for each restart, so the reader can see why one deletion produced 3 restarts. Otherwise, rerun phase 2 with 45 s spacing, so only the receiver changes.

technical: The explanation for the checkpoint gap doesn't fit its size. With checkpoints every 5 s, a scrape inside a 10 s point is off by at most about 2 checkpoints at each instant. The gap was 5 (53 vs 58), and the post presents the explanation as fact. Fix: Show the raw Splunk points and REST samples at tb and te, and work out the largest offset the timing could cause. If 5 is beyond it, say the cause is unknown and present it as an open item, not an explanation.

technical: Readers can't run the lab from the post, because the repository link doesn't match the lab that ran. Fix: Point the git clone, cd and footer links to the published LAB_URL and slug, and check that the 3-step commands run from that path.

editorial: One sentence makes Splunk the subject of what the Kubernetes view didn't show, when the cause is the 10 s k8s_cluster interval and how Kubernetes replaces pods. Fix: Rewrite it to give the reason and what Splunk makes possible: 'At the chart's 10 s k8s_cluster interval, a 2 s replacement usually falls between reports, and that is why the Flink receiver's restart counter is the signal to watch in Splunk.'

claims.text: Flink's monitoring guide lists restarts and checkpoints among the first metrics to watch
An AWS Managed Flink application can report RUNNING while its job keeps failing and restarting
Flink's own test suite detects restarts with numRestarts
Flink marks a job RUNNING when scheduling starts, before every task runs
The Flink receiver is alpha, so metric names can still change
The Flink receiver isn't included in the Splunk distribution of the Collector
The older 'flinkmetrics' receiver type name still works
The chart's k8s_cluster receiver reports every 10 s by default
A dashboard that polls job state every 10 s or more can miss the RESTARTING period entirely
Most of the 17 to 21 s visibility lag comes from the 10 s collection interval and the 5 s batch timeout
A 5 s collection_interval should shorten the lag
The completed-checkpoint gap (53 vs 58) comes from where the scrape falls inside each 10 s point
Deleting a TaskManager pod stands in for a node drain, an eviction or an out-of-memory kill
A detector on the increase of flink.job.restart.count catches restarts that job state and pod health don't show

brief.reader: Data or platform engineer running Apache Flink streaming jobs on Kubernetes, watching them in Splunk Observability Cloud
brief.decision: Whether job state and pod health are enough to know a Flink job is healthy, or whether they need Flink's restart and checkpoint counters in Splunk, and how to get them there
brief.question: My Flink job says RUNNING, so is it fine, and how do I see its restarts and checkpoints in Splunk?
brief.takeaway: When a TaskManager is lost, Flink restarts the job and says RUNNING again, sometimes before every task runs, and Kubernetes replaces the pod rather than restarting a container. Measured on EKS, per deletion: seconds not RUNNING, seconds RUNNING before every task ran and a new checkpoint completed, what Splunk's Kubernetes metrics show, and whether Splunk's flink.job.restart.count from the OpenTelemetry Flink receiver rose by exactly the restarts Flink's REST API counted between the same two instants, with point and arrival lag.
brief.open_question: With a Flink 1.20 job on EKS and a fixed-delay restart strategy, when TaskManager pods are deleted two times without the receiver and three times with it: per deletion, how long is the job not RUNNING and how long does it say RUNNING before every task runs and a new checkpoint completes; what do Splunk's TaskManager Kubernetes metrics show; does Splunk's restart counter rise by exactly the restarts Flink's REST API counts between the same instants; how many seconds until each restart is in a 10-second point and in a 3-second poll; and do checkpoint counters and JobManager and TaskManager GC series arrive?

brief.adds: Flink's monitoring guide, FLINK-34907 and the AWS Managed Flink blog say job state alone hides restarts; Flink's own tests count restarts with numRestarts (FLINK-23807). Splunk's docs show Flink through the Prometheus receiver. This lab runs the OpenTelemetry Flink receiver (contrib 0.165.0) next to the Splunk distribution on EKS, deletes TaskManager pods on purpose, and checks Splunk's counters against Flink's REST API at the same instants, restart by restart.
tradeoffs: The Flink receiver is in the upstream contrib Collector, not the Splunk distribution, so the lab runs a second, small Collector that sends through the Splunk agent
Deleting a TaskManager pod stands in for a node drain, an eviction or an out-of-memory kill; other failure causes are not tested
One job, one TaskManager with two slots, one restart strategy, and a 10-second collection interval; visibility lag depends on that interval
The receiver is alpha; metric names can still change
Kubernetes metrics see pods, not jobs: a deleted pod is replaced by a new one, so the container restart count need not move

demand.evidence: Abhi asked for this topic: he is a code owner of the receiver. FLINK-34907 and the AWS blog above describe a job that says RUNNING while it is not fully running or is restarting. No reaction or view counts were collected.
